tagline: Across Nebraska, an automobile trail follows a corridor shaped by railroads.
intro: The Lincoln Highway Scenic & Historic Byway crosses Nebraska on US 30, a route the Nebraska Department of Transportation identifies as a National Scenic Byway. Visit Nebraska presents the drive through the history of pioneers, cowboys and Pony Express riders, alongside cultural and natural attractions. At North Platte, US 30 follows the north side of the Platte and South Platte rivers; farther east, Columbus occupies flat river-valley ground with rolling hills to its north. Near Sidney, the landscape reaches the western edge of the wheat-growing region; farther west, cattle ranching takes a larger share of the land.

Carl G. Fisher conceived the Lincoln Highway in 1912, and it was dedicated in 1913 as a coast-to-coast automobile route from Times Square to Lincoln Park in San Francisco. The Lincoln Highway Association formed to plan, promote and sign it. Numbered highways gradually replaced the named route after 1926, with much of it becoming US 30. In Columbus, automobile traffic encouraged new garages and hotels, and the city paved and lit downtown streets to attract motorists.

Driving east, begin with Kimball and Sidney, then continue through Ogallala to North Platte. Gothenburg and Lexington lead onward to Kearney and Grand Island. Columbus and Fremont come before Blair at the eastern end of the tourism route. Blair lies in the Loess Hills, surrounded by rolling hills and the Missouri River valley.

moments.title: Ogallala
moments.text: The South Platte runs through Ogallala, a town shaped by cattle trails and the railroad. Cattle driven from Texas met the Union Pacific railhead at Ogallala. The railroad arrived in 1867, before the town was laid out in 1875 and incorporated in 1884. The cattle routes were known as the Western or Great Western trails. In the post office is Frank Mechau’s oil-on-canvas mural Long Horns, painted in 1938. It belongs to the federal mural program run through the Treasury Department’s Section of Painting and Sculpture, later called the Section of Fine Arts.

moments.title: North Platte
moments.text: A locomotive’s maintenance stop gave North Platte time to feed soldiers. Crews lubricated wheels and replenished water while trains paused here. After witnessing an impromptu welcome for troops, Rae Wilson proposed making the train greetings a regular undertaking. The North Platte Canteen operated from Christmas Day 1941 to April 1, 1946, offering refreshments during ten- to fifteen-minute stops. Volunteers came from more than 125 communities, and their groups supplied the day’s food. The canteen continued serving troops returning home after the war. The Lincoln County Historical Museum has a display telling its history.

moments.title: Columbus
moments.text: At Pawnee Park, bronze soldiers step from a life-size replica of a Higgins boat into sand. Columbus was the birthplace of boat designer Andrew Jackson Higgins, the designer of the Landing Craft, Vehicle, Personnel, used in World War II. The Andrew Jackson Higgins National Memorial includes sand from 58 historically significant beaches, including D-Day beaches and beaches in Korea and Vietnam. Another memorial on the same site extends the story beyond those wars: the Freedom Memorial incorporates steel from the World Trade Center, destroyed in the attacks of September 11, 2001.
